newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen getting serious about state divestment.
newsitem.headline: India seen getting serious about state divestment.

text.p: India's ambitious plan to sell $1.4 billion worth of shares in state-owned units in the current fiscal year has gone awry but officials and analysts expect an aggressive sell-off plan in the federal budget later this week.

The analysts said the government must announce a long-term blueprint for sale of shares in the state firms and take into account the recommendations made by a government Disinvestment Commission in its first report submitted on Thursday.

"We hope the government will come out with better results, particularly with the Disinvestment Commission in place," Alok Sethi, director of investment firm Natwest Markets, told Reuters by telephone from Bombay.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram will present the federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.
India, which started partial privatisation under an economic reform programme launched in 1991, set up the commission last year to advise a strategy for disinvestment of shares in 40 state firms.
But disinvestment in the 40 firms is not expected to be taken up before two tranches of sell-offs involving other firms due in the current 1996/97 fiscal year.
The government has set a target of raising 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion) in 1996/97 from divestment, or the sale of partial stakes in state-controlled firms.
Last year India raised 3.57 billion rupees ($99.7 million) from divestment, well short of its target of 70 billion ($1.95 billion).

India had planned to sell a seven percent stake in telecommunications firm Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL) and five percent in oil refiner Indian Oil Corp (IOC) in the first round of divestment in 1996/97.
But the government has not yet fixed a date for kicking off the first round of divestment.
"Political pressures and the stock market conditions affected the disinvestment process this year," said V. Raghuraman, secretary-general of Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham).

Raghuraman said the coalition government was caught in a pincer between free-market advocates and defenders of socialist control, mainly the left parties which are key allies of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government.

"The process will gather momentum once the government puts a proposed policy framework on public sector undertakings (PSUs)," a senior Industry Ministry official, who asked not to be identified, said.
He said the ministry was drafting a bill to give more freedom in decision making to state-owned firms, similar to the suggestions made by the Disinvestment Commission.
"We are going in a systematic manner. Disinvestment is not a unidirectional process which can be applied to all PSUs," G.V. Ramakrishna, chairman of the Disinvestment Commission, said.

The commission on Thursday recommended the sale of stakes in three state-owned firms in the gas, food and tourism industries. Ramakrishna suggested that the government must make unit-specific recommendations in its disinvestment programme.
"The Disinvestment Commission is currently on the right track," said Sethi.
Sethi expected the government to garner 50 billion rupees from the sale of shares in state firms in the 1997/98 budget.
Analysts urged the government to use proceeds from the sale of shares for modernising state-owned firms and not for plugging its fiscal deficit.
India's fiscal deficit is projected at 5.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the current fiscal year ending March 31, against 5.9 percent in the previous year.
